issues.note: Another window with no ED drug RCTs. The EM picks are a pooled andexanet safety analysis from ANNEXA-I and ANNEXA-4, a decade of antidote shortage data, a lipid emulsion review for TCA poisoning, national prehospital buprenorphine data, a sepsis-alert diagnostic study, an albuterol nebulizer comparison and an alcohol withdrawal return-visit cohort. A Danish oral-vs-IV antibiotic trial after appendectomy rounds out the issue.
bottom_line: About 1 in 10 andexanet-treated patients had a thrombotic event, mostly arterial and within the first few days. Prior MI, older age, female sex and high-dose eligibility raised the risk, and restarting anticoagulation was linked to fewer clots.

Antidote shortages are now the norm: 13% of all US drug shortages over 10 years hit toxicology agents, they lasted a median of about a year, and the backup drug was also short in 94% of cases. Physostigmine and dimercaprol have been discontinued.

Lipid emulsion for TCA poisoning rests on 42 published cases. It helped blood pressure more often than QRS widening, so sodium bicarbonate stays first-line and ILE is a rescue option for refractory toxicity.

articles.takeaway: About 10% of andexanet-treated patients clotted; prior MI and high-dose eligibility flagged arterial events
articles.title: Predictors of Thrombotic Events and Mortality in Patients Treated With Andexanet: A Pooled Analysis.
articles.population: 741 andexanet-treated adults with acute major bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor (80% intracranial), ANNEXA-I and ANNEXA-4
articles.summary: Thrombotic events occurred in 10.4% and death in 19.8%. Arterial events came early (median 3.5 days) and venous events later (median 14 days). No baseline factor predicted all thrombotic events, but arterial events were more likely with prior MI (HR 2.64), eligibility for the high-dose regimen (HR 2.44), female sex (HR 1.78) and older age. An arterial event was linked to higher mortality (HR 2.68), and restarting anticoagulation after reversal was associated with fewer thrombotic events.
articles.why: When choosing between andexanet and 4F-PCC for a factor Xa inhibitor bleed, a history of MI or a recent large or late apixaban/rivaroxaban dose (the high-dose criteria) adds clot risk to the decision. After reversal, pharmacists can push for a documented plan to restart anticoagulation once bleeding is controlled.

articles.takeaway: Toxicology drug shortages lasted a median of about a year, and the alternative was usually short too
articles.title: Shortages of agents used to treat poisoning from 2014 to 2024.
articles.population: 1,670 US drug shortages in the University of Utah Drug Information Service database, 2014–2024
articles.summary: Antidotes and key supportive agents made up 223 shortages (13.4%), and 41 were still unresolved at the end of 2024. New toxicology shortages peaked at 30 in 2018, but ongoing shortages outnumbered new ones every year, with a median duration of 12.6 months. Almost all were generic (96%) and parenteral (79%), sedative-hypnotics were hit most often, and manufacturing problems were the usual cause. A therapeutic alternative existed in 83% of cases, but that alternative was itself in shortage 94% of the time.
articles.why: ED pharmacists should keep a current antidote shortage list with pre-approved substitutes and dosing, and know regional sharing options through the poison center. Physostigmine and dimercaprol are discontinued, so plan now for anticholinergic delirium (e.g., benzodiazepines, dexmedetomidine) and heavy-metal chelation alternatives.

articles.takeaway: Lipid emulsion for TCA poisoning helped hypotension more often than QRS widening, but evidence is case reports only
articles.title: The Effect of Intravenous Lipid Emulsion in Tricyclic Antidepressant Poisoning: A Systematic Review.
articles.population: 24 publications (20 case reports, 4 case series), 42 adults with TCA poisoning given IV lipid emulsion
articles.summary: Survival was reported in 41 of 42 cases, including every documented cardiac arrest, though all patients also got other resuscitative treatments. Hypotension resolved in 14 of 17 cases (82%), but wide QRS resolved in only 6 of 14 (43%) and arrhythmias in 4 of 9 (44%). Reported harms included ARDS, hypertriglyceridemia with lab interference and mild liver abnormalities. With no comparator groups and strong publication bias, the authors say ILE can't be called effective or safe for routine use.
articles.why: Sodium bicarbonate (1–2 mEq/kg boluses, targeting QRS narrowing and pH around 7.45–7.55) stays first-line for TCA cardiotoxicity. ILE (20%, 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion) is a rescue option for refractory shock or arrest, and labs should be drawn before it when possible because lipemia interferes with them.

articles.takeaway: Prehospital buprenorphine rose from 33 to over 1,500 EMS doses a year, and 80% of patients improved
articles.title: Prehospital Buprenorphine: A National Cross-Sectional Analysis.
articles.population: 2,180 EMS encounters with buprenorphine given, out of about 167 million US EMS patient contacts, 2020–2023
articles.summary: EMS buprenorphine use climbed from 33 administrations in 2020 to 1,574 in 2023, with a sharp jump starting in spring 2022. Patients were mostly men (62%) with a mean age of 37, about half the doses came during 911 responses, and nearly all were given by paramedics or community paramedics. Initial doses were usually 8 mg (45%) or 16 mg (36%). Most patients improved (80%) and only 4 (0.2%) got worse, and just 16% of 911 patients were transported to a hospital.
articles.why: More patients will arrive having already had 8–24 mg of buprenorphine in the field, so ask EMS for the dose and time before giving more or starting a full agonist. It also strengthens the case for ED-initiated buprenorphine with a bridge prescription and naloxone at discharge.

articles.takeaway: Showing a host-protein bacterial/viral test in the ED sepsis alert led to fewer cefepime doses in unlikely sepsis
articles.title: Integrating a Host-Protein Bacterial/Viral Test into the Emergency Department Sepsis Alert Order Set Is Associated with Changes in Sepsis Category Distribution and Patient Management: A Pre/Postimplementation Study.
articles.population: 893 adults who triggered the ED sepsis alert, 1 US academic medical center, Sept 2024–Mar 2025
articles.summary: The MeMed BV test was ordered automatically in both periods, but clinicians could only see results after implementation. Afterward, more patients were classified as unlikely sepsis (41.1% vs 32.5%) and fewer as possible sepsis (13.2% vs 18.4%). Among unlikely-sepsis patients, mean cefepime doses fell from 3.3 to 2.2 and hospitalization dropped from 92.1% to 79.9%. It's a short, single-center before-and-after study that also included clinician education.
articles.why: A bacterial/viral host-response score could help ED pharmacists question continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics in low-probability sepsis after the first dose. It shouldn't delay that first dose in patients who look septic.

articles.takeaway: Mesh and breath-actuated nebulizers delivered albuterol more than 80% faster than a jet nebulizer
articles.title: High-efficiency Nebulizers Reduce Albuterol Administration Time in the Emergency Department.
articles.population: 296 ED patients aged 3 and older (26% pediatric) getting nebulized albuterol for asthma, 1 US urban Level I trauma center, 2019–2023
articles.summary: A continuous jet nebulizer (single 15 mg dose) took a mean of 60.6 minutes, compared with 12.3 minutes for a vibrating mesh device and about 8 minutes for breath-actuated or breath-enhanced devices given in 5 mg increments up to 15 mg. Adjusted treatment time was 82–88% shorter with the high-efficiency devices. Admission rates, asthma severity scores and peak flow didn't differ between devices. Device assignment wasn't randomized.
articles.why: Faster devices can save about 45 minutes per treatment without changing outcomes, which matters for crowded EDs. Pharmacists and respiratory therapy should coordinate albuterol dosing with the device, since efficient nebulizers deliver more drug per mg and can allow dose-titrated increments.

articles.takeaway: Social and psychiatric factors, not discharge tapers, predicted early ED returns after alcohol withdrawal
articles.title: Factors Associated with Early ED Return Among Patients Discharged After Treatment for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome.
articles.population: 318 ED encounters for alcohol withdrawal discharged home, 1 US academic center, 2020–2023
articles.summary: Fourteen patients (4.4%) returned within 72 hours and 32 (10.1%) were admitted within 30 days. In adjusted models, schizophrenia (OR 8.59), Medicaid insurance (OR 4.43) and anxiety (OR 3.53) predicted 72-hour return, and homelessness predicted 30-day admission (OR 3.19). Discharge taper prescriptions weren't associated with either outcome. The study was small, single-center and had few events.
articles.why: A discharge benzodiazepine or gabapentin taper alone doesn't seem to prevent bounce-backs. Pair it with relapse-prevention medication (naltrexone, acamprosate or gabapentin), thiamine, and social work or addiction follow-up for patients with these risk factors.

articles.takeaway: Three days of oral antibiotics after surgery for complicated appendicitis was noninferior to IV
articles.title: Oral versus intravenous postoperative antibiotics after laparoscopic appendectomy following complicated appendicitis: an open-label cluster-randomized cluster-crossover multiperiod non-inferiority study.
articles.population: 1,021 adults after laparoscopic appendectomy for complicated appendicitis, 12 Danish hospitals
articles.summary: Hospitals alternated between a 3-day oral and a 3-day IV postoperative antibiotic regimen. Intra-abdominal abscess at 30 days occurred in 6.8% with oral vs 4.9% with IV therapy (difference 1.9 points, 90% CI −0.4 to 4.2), meeting the 5-point noninferiority margin, with similar per-protocol results. Oral antibiotics cut hospital stay by about 41 hours but raised readmissions by 4.7 points.
articles.why: Adds to the evidence for short, early-oral courses after source control in intra-abdominal infection, a key stewardship lever. The higher readmission rate argues for clear return precautions and follow-up when patients go home on oral therapy.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window. The EM picks are a systematic review of ED analgesia RCTs, a status epilepticus paralytic comparison, a pilot sepsis bundle trial, a JAMA stroke treatment review, a post hoc tirofiban analysis and national EMS naloxone data. A sepsis procalcitonin meta-analysis and an ED adverse drug reaction study fill out the issue.
bottom_line: For ED acute pain, nonopioid combinations held up against opioid-first regimens across 17 RCTs: ibuprofen plus acetaminophen for musculoskeletal pain, prochlorperazine plus diphenhydramine for migraine, and NSAIDs or IV acetaminophen for renal colic.

When intubating for status epilepticus, a rocuronium-type paralytic was linked to better discharge function than succinylcholine, with no difference in peri-intubation arrhythmias. It's observational, but it removes the main argument for 'sux so you can see the seizure'.
Early tirofiban after IV lytics looked helpful only in moderate-to-severe stroke (NIHSS 6 or more). In minor stroke it added no benefit and raised intracranial bleeding.

articles.takeaway: Multimodal nonopioid analgesia matched or beat opioid-first regimens for common ED pain complaints
articles.title: Multimodal Nonopioid Analgesia Versus Opioid-First Approaches for Acute Pain in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.population: 17 RCTs, 7,288 adults treated in EDs for musculoskeletal or trauma pain, renal colic or primary headache
articles.summary: Most of the evidence (13 trials, about 5,250 patients) involved musculoskeletal trauma, where ibuprofen plus acetaminophen relieved pain about as well as an opioid plus acetaminophen. In migraine, prochlorperazine plus diphenhydramine left 86% with mild or no headache at 1 hour vs 52% with hydromorphone. For renal colic, IM diclofenac and IV acetaminophen were as good as or better than morphine, with fewer adverse events. Results were synthesized descriptively rather than pooled, so they should be read condition by condition.
articles.why: Gives evidence for nonopioid-first ED order sets by complaint: an NSAID plus acetaminophen for sprains and fractures, a dopamine antagonist plus diphenhydramine for migraine, and ketorolac or diclofenac for renal colic. Check renal function, bleeding risk and anticholinergic burden in older adults.

articles.takeaway: Non-depolarizing paralytics for status epilepticus RSI were linked to better discharge function than succinylcholine
articles.title: Neurologic outcomes following intubation with non-depolarizing vs. depolarizing paralytics in status epilepticus: a target trial emulation.
articles.population: 480 adults intubated for suspected status epilepticus, 1 US academic health system, 2000–2024
articles.summary: The authors expected that succinylcholine's short duration, which lets clinicians re-examine the patient sooner, would improve outcomes. After propensity weighting, the opposite appeared: succinylcholine was linked to more need for a higher level of care at discharge (30.4% vs 24.4%; OR 1.35) and fewer discharges home (61.7% vs 69.6%; OR 0.71). Life-threatening peri-intubation arrhythmias were rare and similar (0.6% vs 0.8%). The study spans 24 years at one system and used escalation of care as a stand-in for neurologic outcome.
articles.why: Supports rocuronium as a reasonable RSI choice in status epilepticus, as long as the team doesn't rely on the motor exam afterward: get continuous EEG early and keep antiseizure drugs and sedation going. Sugammadex can reverse rocuronium if an exam is needed.

articles.takeaway: Triggering the sepsis Hour-1 bundle by NEWS2 score raised antibiotic and culture compliance, but outcomes stayed uncertain
articles.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS).
articles.population: 200 adults admitted with infection and NEWS2 of 5 or more, 4 EDs in Hong Kong
articles.summary: EDs switched in a randomized sequence to automatically starting the Hour-1 bundle (lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors as needed) whenever NEWS2 reached 5. Compliance with lactate, blood cultures and antibiotics rose, but full bundle compliance was only 56%. Thirty-day mortality was 3.9% with standard care vs 9.2% with the new model, a difference that wasn't significant (95% CI −1.6 to 12.1 points). The pilot met its feasibility goals, and the authors say a much larger trial is needed.
articles.why: An objective score can get antibiotics hung faster, but this pilot can't show it helps patients and the mortality numbers leaned the wrong way. ED pharmacists can still own the antibiotic step: first dose within the hour, with culture draws coordinated so they don't delay it.

articles.takeaway: JAMA review lays out 2026 AHA/ASA stroke care: tenecteplase or alteplase within 4.5 hours, extended windows with imaging
articles.title: Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Review.
articles.population: Clinical review based on 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guidelines
articles.summary: IV thrombolysis with tenecteplase or alteplase is first-line for disabling stroke within 4.5 hours of onset when there are no contraindications, and adds about 10 percentage points to the chance of a better functional outcome. Perfusion imaging can extend lytics to 9 hours, and up to 24 hours for large-vessel occlusions that can't go to thrombectomy. Thrombectomy is a class 1 recommendation within 6 hours and in selected patients up to 24 hours, and adds about 20 points of functional independence. Lytics should still be given first in thrombectomy candidates unless contraindicated.
articles.why: A current one-stop reference for stroke code pharmacists. Know tenecteplase dosing (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg, single bolus) vs alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg, 10% bolus), and the newer extended-window criteria that widen who qualifies.

articles.takeaway: Early tirofiban after IV lytics helped moderate-to-severe strokes but raised bleeding without benefit in minor strokes
articles.title: Association of Stroke Severity With Efficacy of Early Tirofiban Infusion After Intravenous Thrombolysis.
articles.population: 832 patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke given IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours, ASSET-IT trial (China)
articles.summary: Patients were split by NIHSS at admission (under 6 vs 6 or more). With NIHSS of 6 or more, tirofiban roughly doubled the odds of an excellent 90-day outcome (mRS 0–1; aOR 2.13) without a clear rise in intracranial hemorrhage (aOR 0.88). With minor stroke, there was no benefit (aOR 1.02) and intracranial hemorrhage rose (aOR 6.51, very wide CI). Interactions were significant, but this was an exploratory subgroup analysis.
articles.why: If your stroke team is adopting early tirofiban after lytics, this argues for restricting it to NIHSS 6 or more. Pharmacists building the protocol should include a severity cutoff, renal dose adjustment and a plan for holding it if neuro status worsens.

articles.takeaway: EMS naloxone use in suspected opioid overdose was about twice as likely in the South and Midwest as in the Northeast
articles.title: A national cross-sectional analysis of regional and rural-urban variation in emergency medical services naloxone administration for suspected opioid overdose.
articles.population: 110,261 EMS activations for suspected opioid involvement in adults, US national 2025 dataset
articles.summary: EMS gave naloxone in 33.9% of encounters. After clinical adjustment, odds were higher in the South (aOR 2.10), Midwest (aOR 1.92) and West (aOR 1.31) than in the Northeast, about 5 to 15 percentage points. The rural-urban gap disappeared after adjustment (aOR 1.01). The authors note the data can't show whether any given non-administration was inappropriate.
articles.why: EMS naloxone counts are often used to track overdose trends, and regional practice differences can distort them. In the ED, ask what prehospital naloxone was given and how much, because it shapes the observation period for long-acting opioids.

articles.takeaway: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotics shortened therapy by about 1.5 days in ICU sepsis without changing mortality
articles.title: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic therapy in ICU patients with sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with GRADE and trial sequential analysis.
articles.population: 16 RCTs, 7,966 adult ICU patients with sepsis or septic shock
articles.summary: Procalcitonin-guided strategies didn't change all-cause mortality (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.92–1.06), and trial sequential analysis said the evidence was still inconclusive on that question. They cut antibiotic duration by about 1.5 days (MD −1.51), a result trial sequential analysis judged conclusive, and increased antibiotic-free days. New infections, superinfections, clinical failure and length of stay didn't differ.
articles.why: Supports procalcitonin as a stop signal, not a start signal: it doesn't decide whether to give the first ED dose, but a falling level helps stewardship pharmacists shorten courses safely once patients are admitted.

articles.takeaway: Diuretic-related ED admissions rose steeply once 5-day mean temperatures passed about 16 °C
articles.title: Diuretic-associated admissions to the emergency department - too hot to handle? Results from the ADRED-study.
articles.population: ED admissions with standardized ADR causality assessment, prospective multicenter German ADRED study
articles.summary: Researchers compared 5-day mean ambient temperature with the share of diuretic users admitted for a suspected diuretic adverse reaction. Higher temperatures were associated with more diuretic ADRs, and segmented regression found a breakpoint near 15.7 °C, above which the slope increased about sixfold. Spline models also showed an accelerating, non-linear rise. The study can't separate the individual mechanisms, such as dehydration, hyponatremia or AKI.
articles.why: During heat waves, diuretic users presenting with AKI, hyponatremia, hypokalemia or falls should prompt a look at their dose. ED pharmacists can recommend temporary dose reductions or 'sick day' holds at discharge in hot weather.

issues.note: Another window with no ED drug RCTs. The EM picks are a large stroke-mimic thrombolysis meta-analysis, a 12-month DOAC-after-ICH registry, two toxicology surveillance studies and two ED pharmacotherapy evidence reviews. A big NEJM VTE prophylaxis trial and a BMJ perioperative ACE inhibitor/ARB trial round out the issue.
bottom_line: Don't let fear of treating a stroke mimic slow down tenecteplase or alteplase: across about 285,000 patients, mimics who got lytics had far less ICH and death than true strokes.

Tianeptine was the top substance in a decade of poison center withdrawal calls and drove more than a quarter of the ICU admissions. Ask about gas-station supplements when withdrawal doesn't fit a known drug.
Muscle relaxants don't improve recovery from acute low back pain in ED patients, so leave them off routine discharge prescriptions.

articles.takeaway: Stroke mimics given IV thrombolysis had far less intracranial bleeding and death than true ischemic strokes
articles.title: Safety and clinical outcomes of intravenous thrombolysis in stroke mimics compared with acute ischemic stroke: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 27 cohort studies and 1 RCT, about 285,000 adults given IV thrombolysis for suspected stroke
articles.summary: Compared with confirmed ischemic stroke, mimics who got lytics had much lower odds of symptomatic ICH (OR 0.18), any ICH (OR 0.12) and 3-month death (OR 0.24). They were also more likely to be functionally independent at 3 months (OR 3.50) and to go home, and stays were about 2 days shorter. The ICH gap was widest in patients with milder deficits (NIHSS 7 or less). The better outcomes reflect how benign mimics are, not a benefit of the drug, and the data are almost entirely observational.
articles.why: Supports keeping door-to-needle times fast instead of holding lytics while waiting for diagnostic certainty. Pharmacists can reinforce that a mimic diagnosis afterward isn't a medication error, while still running the usual pre-lytic checks (BP, glucose, anticoagulant history).

articles.takeaway: Restarting a DOAC within 14 days of ICH in AF carried more later hemorrhagic than ischemic stroke at 1 year
articles.title: Early Direct Oral Anticoagulant Initiation After Intracranial Hemorrhage Among Japanese Patients With Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation: SAFE-ICH Registry 12-Month Outcomes.
articles.population: 240 adults with nonvalvular AF who started or restarted a DOAC 14 days or less after ICH, 32 Japanese hospitals
articles.summary: Over 12 months, symptomatic ICH, any stroke or death occurred in 22.5% (29.1 per 100 person-years). Symptomatic ICH occurred in 6.3%, hemorrhagic stroke in 3.8% and ischemic stroke in 2.9%, with major bleeding in 6.7% and death in 14.2%, mostly from aspiration pneumonia. Hemorrhagic strokes began appearing about 3 months after the DOAC started and caught up with ischemic strokes by month 10. There was no comparison group of delayed or no anticoagulation.
articles.why: Early DOAC restart after ICH is still a case-by-case call, and this suggests the bleeding risk persists well beyond the first month. When these patients return to the ED, check DOAC dose appropriateness and have andexanet or 4F-PCC protocols ready.

articles.takeaway: Pregabalin overdoses in Australia fell by almost half after media coverage, prescribing limits and boxed warnings
articles.title: Changes in pregabalin use and overdose after government interventions and media coverage: retrospective observational study.
articles.population: 227,864 people dispensed pregabalin (10% national dispensing sample) and 4,871 pregabalin overdose calls to Australia's largest poisons centre, 2016–2024
articles.summary: Dispensing peaked in 2018 and then dropped at three breakpoints that lined up with media coverage (Dec 2018), prescribing and dispensing restrictions (2020) and, after a delay, boxed warnings (2021), for a combined dispensing rate ratio of 0.75. Overdose calls fell further, with a combined rate ratio of 0.53 and an ongoing decline of about 1.6% a month. A high-risk group of about 14% of users were younger, mostly male, filled prescriptions more often, and commonly also took opioids (66%) or benzodiazepines (32%).
articles.why: Gabapentinoids add to respiratory depression with opioids and benzodiazepines, a pattern that also shows up in US overdoses. In the ED, flag pregabalin plus opioid or benzodiazepine combinations at med rec and avoid starting pregabalin at discharge for acute pain.

articles.takeaway: Tianeptine led a decade of poison center withdrawal calls and caused more than a quarter of ICU admissions
articles.title: Withdrawal-related calls to a statewide poison control center: a ten-year review.
articles.population: 198 withdrawal-related calls to one US statewide poison control center, 2015–2024
articles.summary: Tianeptine (24%), opioids (21%) and benzodiazepines (14%) were the most common substances, and tianeptine calls first appeared in 2019 and drove a rise starting in 2020. Most calls came from hospitals, and 37% of cases had at least a moderate outcome. About a third of patients were admitted and 18% went to the ICU, with tianeptine linked to 28% of ICU admissions. GHB and phenibut withdrawal also had notable moderate or major outcomes, and no deaths were recorded.
articles.why: Tianeptine is sold as a supplement and acts on mu-opioid receptors, so withdrawal looks like opioid withdrawal and may respond to buprenorphine or methadone. GHB and phenibut withdrawal can look like severe alcohol withdrawal and may need high-dose benzodiazepines or phenobarbital. Call poison control early.

articles.takeaway: IV magnesium is first-line for eclampsia and torsades but only an adjunct for migraine, AF and asthma
articles.title: Applications of intravenous magnesium Sulfate in the emergency department: A narrative review.
articles.population: Review of the evidence for IV magnesium sulfate in adult ED indications
articles.summary: The authors rank the evidence by indication. Magnesium remains first-line for preeclampsia and eclampsia and the drug of choice for torsades de pointes. It plays a supporting role in migraine and as an add-on for rate control in AF with RVR, and should be saved for severe asthma or COPD exacerbations that don't respond to initial therapy. Routine empiric use for hypokalemia isn't recommended, evidence for analgesia is limited, and it may help shivering during targeted temperature management. No serious adverse events were reported in the studies reviewed.
articles.why: A handy reference for common ED orders. Typical doses are 2 g IV for torsades or asthma and a 4–6 g load then 1–2 g/h for eclampsia. Watch reflexes, respiratory rate and renal function, and keep calcium gluconate available for magnesium toxicity.

articles.takeaway: Muscle relaxants don't improve symptoms or function in ED patients with acute low back pain
articles.title: Are Muscle Relaxants an Effective Treatment for Patients With Acute Low Back Pain?
articles.population: 4 RCTs and 2 meta-analyses of muscle relaxants for acute low back pain, including ED patients
articles.summary: This structured clinical question review found that muscle relaxants didn't improve symptom resolution or function in ED patients with acute low back pain. The authors weighed that lack of benefit against side effects such as sedation and dizziness. They conclude that muscle relaxants shouldn't be prescribed routinely from the ED for this condition.
articles.why: Cyclobenzaprine and similar drugs are common discharge add-ons with sedation, fall and misuse risks, particularly in older adults and in combination with opioids. An NSAID plus activity and heat is the better default, and pharmacists can drop muscle relaxants from back pain order sets.

articles.takeaway: Aspirin wasn't noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin for preventing death or VTE after hip or knee replacement
articles.title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement.
articles.population: 18,883 patients randomized after elective hip or knee arthroplasty, 15,317 in the per-protocol analysis, US (PEPPER)
articles.summary: Patients got aspirin 81 mg twice daily, warfarin (INR target 2.0) or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 30 days. Death or symptomatic VTE at 6 months occurred in 1.26% with aspirin, 1.23% with warfarin and 0.94% with rivaroxaban, and aspirin didn't meet the 0.69-point noninferiority margin against either drug. Bleeding, wound reoperation or MI occurred in 2.91%, 3.36% and 3.48%, and the anticoagulants weren't noninferior to aspirin for safety either. Absolute differences were small in every comparison.
articles.why: There's no clear winner: aspirin trades slightly more clots for slightly less bleeding. Patients presenting to the ED after arthroplasty could be on any of these agents, so confirm which one and the dose before working up a DVT or a bleed.

articles.takeaway: Holding the morning ACE inhibitor or ARB before surgery cut perioperative hypotension in older adults
articles.title: Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial.
articles.population: 2,036 adults aged 60–80 on an ACE inhibitor or ARB having non-cardiac surgery under general anesthesia, 5 Chinese hospitals
articles.summary: Patients got their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a matching placebo on the morning of surgery. Perioperative hypotension occurred in 31.2% after holding the dose vs 45.5% after taking it (aOR 0.52, absolute difference −14.4 points). Vasopressor use and hypotension duration were also lower, while postoperative hypotension, 30-day complications and mortality didn't differ. The trial wasn't powered for rarer clinical outcomes.
articles.why: Strong evidence to hold ACE inhibitors and ARBs the morning of surgery in older adults. The same logic applies when ED patients go for emergency procedures or RSI: a recent ACE inhibitor or ARB dose is a reason to expect hypotension and have a vasopressor ready.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window. The EM picks are a large secondary analysis of two airway trials, a peripheral vasopressor extravasation series, an ACMT naloxone position statement, and inpatient analgesia and stroke anticoagulation cohorts. One ICU analgesia RCT and two pharmacist-relevant studies fill out the issue.
bottom_line: In pooled DEVICE and PREOXI data, ketamine induction was linked to more peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse than etomidate (20% vs 14%), mainly new or higher vasopressor needs. It wasn't randomized, but it argues against assuming ketamine is the hemodynamically safer choice.
Expired naloxone is better than no naloxone: ACMT now says to give it when an unexpired product isn't on hand.
When peripheral vasopressors infiltrated and phentolamine was given, serious tissue injury was rare (2 of 92), even though phentolamine came a mean of about 2 hours after the event.

articles.takeaway: Ketamine was linked to more peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse than etomidate in critically ill adults
articles.title: Ketamine Vs. Etomidates and Cardiovascular Collapse During Emergency Tracheal Intubation: A Secondary Analysis of the DEVICE and PREOXI Trials.
articles.population: 2,357 adults intubated in US EDs and ICUs (1,822 etomidate, 312 ketamine, 223 other), DEVICE and PREOXI trials
articles.summary: Induction drug choice wasn't randomized, so the authors treated it as an observational exposure and used weighting and covariate adjustment. Cardiovascular collapse (new or increased vasopressor, SBP under 65 mm Hg or arrest within 2 minutes of intubation) occurred in 20.4% with ketamine vs 14.0% with etomidate (aOR 1.80, 95% CI 1.24–2.62), driven mostly by vasopressor starts or increases (aOR 1.51). Ketamine showed less severe hypoxemia and faster intubation, but neither held up after correcting for multiple comparisons, and first-pass success and 28-day mortality didn't clearly differ.
articles.why: Echoes the RSI trial signal that ketamine isn't automatically the safer agent in shock. Whichever drug is used, consider a reduced dose in unstable patients and have push-dose or infusion vasopressors drawn up before induction.

articles.takeaway: Serious tissue injury was rare after peripheral vasopressor extravasation treated with phentolamine
articles.title: Local complications of peripheral intravenous vasopressor use with phentolamine as an antidote: a retrospective review.
articles.population: 92 patients given phentolamine for infiltrated peripheral vasopressor IVs, 1 large US health system
articles.summary: Infiltration happened a mean of 21 hours into peripheral vasopressor therapy, most often at antecubital or forearm sites, and phentolamine was given a mean of 131 minutes later. Three-quarters of patients had no significant tissue injury and about a quarter had only minor bruising or redness. There were two significant complications (one skin necrosis and one DVT), and 52% went on to get a central line. The study included only patients who received phentolamine, so it can't give an overall extravasation rate.
articles.why: Supports peripheral norepinephrine as a bridge from the ED, paired with a protocol for site checks and phentolamine (commonly 5–10 mg diluted in 10 mL saline, injected subcutaneously around the site). The 2-hour delay to phentolamine shows room to stock it closer to the bedside.

articles.takeaway: ACMT says to give expired naloxone for suspected opioid overdose when unexpired naloxone isn't available
articles.title: ACMT Position Statement: Administer Expired Naloxone When Unexpired Naloxone Is Unavailable.
articles.population: American College of Medical Toxicology guidance for clinicians, first responders and lay rescuers
articles.summary: The American College of Medical Toxicology states that expired naloxone should be given for a suspected opioid overdose if no unexpired product is available. PubMed lists no abstract, so the detailed rationale isn't summarized here. Naloxone is generally regarded as a stable drug with a very favorable safety profile, so the risk of using an expired product is low compared with giving nothing.
articles.why: Useful for naloxone kit counseling at ED discharge: patients shouldn't throw out an expired kit until they have a replacement. It also supports keeping older kits in community distribution rather than discarding them outright.

articles.takeaway: Inpatient ibuprofen raised AKI risk vs oxycodone only in high-risk patients, not in low-risk ones
articles.title: Ibuprofen Use and Acute Kidney Injury Among Adults Admitted to the Hospital.
articles.population: 78,656 hospitalized adults treated at least 24 hours with ibuprofen (6,313) or oxycodone (72,343), 3 Philadelphia hospitals, 2004–2017
articles.summary: After weighting, ibuprofen was associated with more AKI (IRR 1.22), severe AKI (IRR 1.36) and kidney replacement therapy (IRR 3.29, wide CI), and most AKI was stage 1. The excess risk was concentrated in postoperative (IRR 1.70) and critically ill (IRR 1.65) patients. In low-risk patients (under 60, not critically ill or postoperative, normal kidney function), ibuprofen showed no added AKI risk (IRR 0.94), yet most of them got oxycodone.
articles.why: Supports NSAID-first analgesia for low-risk admitted and ED patients rather than reflexive opioids. Reserve caution for the groups where risk was real: post-op, critically ill, older or with reduced kidney function.

articles.takeaway: Starting anticoagulation within 7 days of moderate-severe ischemic stroke didn't raise 30-day bleeding
articles.title: Timing of Anticoagulant Initiation After Moderate-Severe and Severe Acute Ischemic Strokes (TAMSS).
articles.population: 143 neuro-ICU adults with moderate-severe or severe ischemic stroke and an anticoagulation indication, 1 US tertiary center, 2019–2024
articles.summary: Early anticoagulation (within 7 days of onset, 91 patients) was compared with late initiation (after 7 days, 52 patients). Major extracranial bleeding or symptomatic ICH within 30 days occurred in 12% vs 10% (p = 0.78), and recurrent stroke, embolism and mortality at 30 and 90 days didn't differ. Concurrent P2Y12 inhibitor use was the main predictor of bleeding (OR 5.2). The sample was small and timing was chosen by clinicians.
articles.why: Adds to ELAN and TIMING data that early DOAC starts are reasonable even in larger strokes. The P2Y12 signal is a cue for pharmacists to question dual antithrombotic therapy when anticoagulation begins.

articles.takeaway: Pip-tazo and cefepime had similar mortality for Enterobacter, K. aerogenes and Citrobacter bacteremia
articles.title: Real-world outcomes of Citrobacter freundii, Klebsiella aerogenes, and Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia treatment (ROCKET): a contemporary analysis of treatment strategies.
articles.population: 728 adults with bacteremia from moderate AmpC-risk Enterobacterales, multicenter US, 2017–2025
articles.summary: Definitive therapy was cefepime in 47%, pip-tazo in 18% and a carbapenem in 16%, and overall 30-day mortality was 12%. After weighting, 30-day mortality didn't differ between pip-tazo and cefepime (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.57–1.92), and early relapse was similar. Treatment-emergent resistance was uncommon with every agent (1–3%).
articles.why: IDSA guidance favors cefepime for these organisms, and this is reassuring data if a patient started on pip-tazo in the ED is already improving. It doesn't argue for switching the default away from cefepime.

articles.takeaway: Oliceridine matched remifentanil for ICU analgesia with less respiratory depression
articles.title: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
articles.population: 304 mechanically ventilated adults, 19 ICUs in China
articles.summary: Both opioids were titrated to a CPOT score under 3. Median time in the target analgesia range was 96.0% with oliceridine vs 92.3% with remifentanil, meeting non-inferiority. Oliceridine had fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (IRR 0.72) and no respiratory depression during the study or after extubation (0% vs 4.6% and 0% vs 7.9%). Ventilation time, ICU stay and 28-day mortality didn't differ.
articles.why: A G protein-biased opioid could suit ventilated patients nearing extubation, but US availability and cost are limiting, and the trial compared it with remifentanil rather than the more common fentanyl or hydromorphone infusions.

articles.takeaway: Potential drug interactions were found in 89% of ED admissions, and real interaction harm caused 6% of admissions
articles.title: Drug-drug interactions in patients admitted to the hospital: prevalence and associated adverse drug events.
articles.population: 968 adults admitted through the ED taking at least 2 medications (median age 75, median 7 drugs), 2018
articles.summary: Screening home medications with Micromedex, UpToDate and Stockley found 7,801 moderate-or-worse potential interactions in 89% of patients. Only 1.5% of those (116) caused a documented adverse event, but those events contributed to admission in 6% of patients. Most were bleeding events, and antithrombotics were the most common culprits.
articles.why: Most interaction alerts are noise, but antithrombotic combinations are where real harm shows up. ED med rec should focus on anticoagulant plus antiplatelet, NSAID or SSRI pairings in older patients.

issues.note: A heavy cardiology window (several NEJM outcome trials landed at once) but a light one for ED pharmacotherapy, with no ED drug RCTs. The EM picks are a toxicology guidance paper, a pediatric resuscitation dosing meta-analysis, a large nonrandomized ECPR study and a BP-target trial in prior stroke.
bottom_line: A suspected medical-aid-in-dying mixture exposure (benzodiazepine or barbiturate, opioid, plus digoxin, beta-blocker or TCA) needs a digoxin level, serial ECGs and poison center input. Have digoxin Fab, high-dose insulin and bicarbonate ready, and avoid flumazenil and reflexive naloxone in the mixed ingestion.

For pediatric resuscitation drug dosing, a habitus-corrected length tape (PAWPER) beat the Broselow tape on weight accuracy, dose accuracy and time to drug, while age-based weight formulas were consistently inaccurate.
Prehospital ECPR by helicopter teams was linked to doubled survival to discharge (40% vs 20%) in refractory OHCA patients 50 or younger, but the study wasn't randomized.

articles.takeaway: Accidental exposure to medical-aid-in-dying drug mixtures is survivable with fast, toxin-specific ED care
articles.title: Unintended Exposure to Medical Aid in Dying Drug Mixtures: Principles of Emergency Care.
articles.population: Narrative review with proposed management principles; US context as MAID expands (New York legalized it in Aug 2026)
articles.summary: MAID mixtures are self-administered at home and typically combine a benzodiazepine and/or barbiturate, an opioid, and a cardiotoxin such as digoxin, a beta-blocker or a TCA, so a child or other unintended person may ingest a partial dose. The authors propose early poison center contact, supportive resuscitation, activated charcoal or gastric aspiration when safe, a serum digoxin level and serial ECGs, and toxin-specific therapy: digoxin immune Fab, high-dose insulin for propranolol, and sodium bicarbonate for TCA-related QRS widening. They advise avoiding flumazenil and naloxone in these mixed ingestions. These are expert recommendations, not trial-based.
articles.why: A new exposure type for ED pharmacists to plan for as more states legalize MAID. Confirm digoxin Fab stock and a high-dose insulin protocol, and remember that reversing sedation can unmask seizures or arrhythmias in a mixed ingestion.

articles.takeaway: A habitus-corrected length tape beat the Broselow tape for pediatric resuscitation weight and dose accuracy
articles.title: Weight Estimation and Dose Calculation in Resuscitation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 250 studies of weight-estimation and dose-calculation tools in children (9 in children actually being resuscitated)
articles.summary: Compared with the Broselow tape, the PAWPER tape (a length-based tape that adds a body-habitus correction) was better for weight accuracy, dose accuracy and time to drug administration in every analysis. In paired comparisons it more than doubled the odds of an estimate within 10% of true weight (OR 2.48, 95% CI 2.04–3.02). Age-based formulas got fewer than half of estimates within 10%. No study reported patient outcomes, and children longer than the tape or with growth problems were often excluded.
articles.why: Weight errors are a leading source of pediatric code dosing mistakes. Supports habitus-adjusted tapes or measured weights over age formulas, paired with pharmacist-verified, pre-calculated dosing references.

articles.takeaway: Helicopter teams that could start ECPR on scene doubled survival to discharge in young refractory OHCA patients
articles.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.population: 231 adults aged 50 or younger with refractory OHCA, nationwide in the Netherlands (OnScene)
articles.summary: Patients attended by ECPR-equipped helicopter EMS teams (144) were compared with those attended by teams without ECPR capability (87). Survival to hospital discharge was 40% vs 20% (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.59–4.66), and favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months was 36% vs 13% (OR 4.22). Adverse events were more frequent with ECPR (32 vs 11). Allocation depended on which team responded, not randomization, so confounding remains possible.
articles.why: As ECPR moves earlier in the chain of survival, pharmacists will own the heparin bolus at cannulation, sedation and vasopressor plans, and post-arrest drug management. Worth knowing for EDs considering ECPR programs.

articles.takeaway: Targeting systolic BP under 120 after ischemic stroke or TIA cut major cardiovascular events by about a fifth
articles.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke.
articles.population: 4,368 adults with elevated BP and prior ischemic stroke or TIA, 30 sites in Brazil (OPTIMAL-STROKE)
articles.summary: In this open-label trial, achieved systolic BP was about 122 vs 135 mm Hg. Over a median of 3.9 years, cardiovascular death, MI, stroke or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure occurred in 10.9% with intensive treatment vs 13.5% with standard treatment (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.94). The composite kidney outcome was more common with intensive treatment, while overall serious adverse events were similar. A companion trial in type 2 diabetes (OPTIMAL-DIABETES, PMID 43001746) found no significant benefit of the same target (HR 0.90).
articles.why: Supports aggressive long-term BP goals once the acute stroke phase is over, which shapes discharge regimens and med counseling. It doesn't apply to acute BP management in the first hours of stroke, and kidney function needs monitoring.

articles.takeaway: Stopping primary-prevention statins in multimorbid adults 70 and older was noninferior at 2 years, but events ran higher
articles.title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease.
articles.population: 1,880 adults aged 70 or older (mean 77.5) with at least two chronic conditions taking statins for primary prevention, international (STREAM)
articles.summary: Participants were randomized to stop or continue statins and other lipid-lowering drugs in an open-label design. The difference in event-free survival time at 2 years was −2.0 weeks (95% CI −3.7 to −0.3), within the −5.2-week noninferiority margin. However, nonfatal MI, nonfatal ischemic stroke or death occurred in 12.7% after stopping vs 9.2% with continuation, and serious adverse events were 43.0% vs 39.8%. Follow-up was only about 2 years.
articles.why: Noninferior isn't the same as harmless: the raw event rates favored continuing. For pharmacists doing deprescribing reviews, stopping is a reasonable shared decision in frail older adults with limited life expectancy, not a default.

articles.takeaway: IL-6 blockade with ziltivekimab lowered inflammation markers but didn't reduce cardiovascular events
articles.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease.
articles.population: 6,376 adults with atherosclerotic CVD, CKD and hs-CRP of 2 mg/L or higher, multinational (ZEUS)
articles.summary: Monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab 15 mg cut free IL-6 by 76 and hs-CRP by 64 percentage points vs placebo at 24 months. Over a median of 33 months, cardiovascular death, MI or stroke occurred in 17.6% vs 17.7% (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88–1.11). Serious infections were somewhat more frequent with ziltivekimab (20.4% vs 17.9%). The trial was funded by Novo Nordisk.
articles.why: A major negative result for the inflammation hypothesis in cardiovascular disease, at least for IL-6 in CKD. Lowering a biomarker didn't translate into fewer events, and infection risk rose.

articles.takeaway: Pelacarsen cut lipoprotein(a) by about 70% but didn't reduce cardiovascular events over almost 5 years
articles.title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).
articles.population: 8,322 adults with established CVD and Lp(a) of 70 mg/dL or higher, international (Lp(a)HORIZON)
articles.summary: Monthly subcutaneous pelacarsen 80 mg lowered median Lp(a) from about 236 to 64 nmol/L at 12 months, while levels stayed near baseline with placebo. Over a median of 4.7 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 12.3% vs 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15), with no benefit in patients with Lp(a) of 90 mg/dL or higher either. Serious adverse events were slightly lower with pelacarsen (37.3% vs 41.1%). The trial was funded by Novartis.
articles.why: The first Lp(a)-lowering outcomes trial was negative, which tempers expectations for the other Lp(a) agents in development. For now, high Lp(a) remains a risk marker that calls for aggressive LDL and BP control.

articles.takeaway: Vitamin A is recommended for confirmed measles, but no US liquid formulation makes it easy to give young children
articles.title: Clinical consultation: The role of vitamin A in the management of confirmed acute measles infection.
articles.population: Review of evidence and practical administration issues amid record 2026 US measles cases
articles.summary: US measles cases in 2026 are the highest in more than 30 years. WHO and the AAP recommend vitamin A for confirmed acute measles, but the US lacks an FDA-approved concentrated liquid, so children who can't swallow capsules need cumbersome extraction methods. The authors advise confirming the diagnosis, screening for drug interactions, and checking for toxicity symptoms in patients who already received vitamin A.
articles.why: Children with measles will show up in the ED. Pharmacists should know the age-based doses (50,000 IU under 6 months, 100,000 IU at 6–11 months, 200,000 IU at 12 months or older, daily for 2 days) and have a plan for preparing doses from capsules.

issues.note: A very quiet Sunday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue is shorter. The EM picks are two retrospective cohorts and a post hoc STEMI analysis, and the rest is a phase 2 trial, a small open-label RCT and pharmacist-practice data. Read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Nebulized TXA for hemoptysis didn't reduce 72-hour rebleeding in a matched ICU cohort, even as its use climbed to 78% of patients. It remains an unproven adjunct until randomized data arrive.

High bleeding risk alone doesn't identify STEMI patients who should skip aspirin at primary PCI: ischemic events ran numerically higher and bleeding numerically lower with prasugrel monotherapy, in both risk groups.
Don't start aspirin for sepsis on the strength of a large MIMIC-IV signal. The authors themselves say the lower early mortality can't be read as causal.

articles.takeaway: Nebulized TXA didn't reduce 72-hour hemoptysis recurrence in ICU patients who didn't need immediate embolization
articles.title: Analysis of tranexamic acid in hemoptysis: effectiveness in a noninterventional evaluation (ATHENE).
articles.population: 228 ICU adults with hemoptysis not needing embolization within 6 hours, 1 center, 2017–2021
articles.summary: A third of patients (75) got nebulized TXA, and its use grew from 0% to 78% over the study. After 1:2 propensity matching, recurrence of at least 50 mL by 72 hours was 10.7% with TXA vs 12.3% without (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.37–2.32), and 30-day recurrence, respiratory failure, embolization and length of stay didn't differ. Thirty-day mortality was higher with TXA (9.3% vs 1.9%; OR 5.9), but events were few and mostly tied to underlying malignancy. Patients bleeding more than 200 mL at admission were excluded.
articles.why: Nebulized TXA has spread faster than its evidence. It is low cost and reasonable to discuss, but it shouldn't delay airway protection, reversal of anticoagulation or embolization, and this cohort is too small to rule out either benefit or harm.

articles.takeaway: Low-dose aspirin in sepsis tracked with lower early mortality, but the authors caution against treating sepsis with it
articles.title: Time-dependent associations of documented low-dose aspirin administration with 28-day mortality and early safety outcomes in adults with sepsis: a MIMIC-IV cohort study.
articles.population: 31,888 adults with Sepsis-3 in a single-center US ICU database; 4,771 got aspirin 75–100 mg
articles.summary: Time-dependent Cox models linked documented enteral aspirin to lower in-hospital mortality during the first 24 hours (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31–0.75) and at 24–72 hours (HR 0.63), with no clear association after that. Restricting to patients whose SOFA qualified by time zero gave similar numbers but a less certain first-day estimate (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.28–1.03). A hemoglobin drop of 2 g/dL or more was slightly more common with early aspirin (RR 1.10), though many of those drops came before the first dose. The analysis had residual imbalance, and prior aspirin exposure was uncertain.
articles.why: Patients well enough to take enteral aspirin differ from those who can't, so survival bias is a real concern. A practical takeaway is narrower: don't reflexively stop home aspirin in septic patients without a bleeding reason.

articles.takeaway: High bleeding risk didn't identify STEMI patients who benefit from skipping aspirin at primary PCI
articles.title: High Bleeding Risk and Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary PCI in STEMI: A Post Hoc Analysis of the PREMIUM Trial.
articles.population: 2,189 Japanese STEMI patients randomized to low-dose prasugrel alone or aspirin plus prasugrel; 786 (36%) met ARC-HBR criteria
articles.summary: High-bleeding-risk patients had more 12-month death, stroke or MI (16.2% vs 6.2%) and more BARC 3 or 5 bleeding (10.9% vs 4.9%) than others. Monotherapy vs DAPT gave ischemic rates of 18.0% vs 14.5% in HBR patients (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.91–1.82) and 7.4% vs 5.0% in non-HBR patients (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.01–2.37), with no significant interaction. Bleeding was numerically lower with monotherapy in both groups (HR 0.71 and 0.62). Precision was limited and the low-dose Japanese prasugrel regimen may not translate elsewhere.
articles.why: Keeps aspirin in the ED STEMI loading routine for now, even for patients at high bleeding risk. Bleeding risk matters more for later de-escalation decisions than for the first dose.

articles.takeaway: DOACs were linked to lower mortality and intracranial bleeding than warfarin for LV thrombus in high-bleeding-risk patients
articles.title: One-Year Comparative Outcomes of Direct Oral Anticoagulants Versus Warfarin In Patients With Left Ventricular Thrombus And High Bleeding Risks.
articles.population: 4,416 matched US adults with LV thrombus and high bleeding risk (2,208 per group), 2013–2023
articles.summary: At 1 year, DOAC use was associated with lower mortality (24.9% vs 29.3%; HR 0.84), systemic embolism (1.9% vs 3.1%; HR 0.58), intracranial hemorrhage (1.3% vs 2.3%; HR 0.56) and hospitalization (72.0% vs 75.5%; HR 0.89). Stroke or TIA, cerebral infarction and major bleeding didn't differ significantly, even though the abstract's conclusion mentions reduced major bleeding. These health-record data can't capture warfarin INR control or DOAC dose appropriateness.
articles.why: Adds support for off-label DOAC use in LV thrombus, which comes up with post-MI patients at ED discharge and on admission. Check renal function and dose carefully in this high-risk group, and note the reported results don't support a major-bleeding advantage.

articles.takeaway: One infusion of either factor XI antibody cut PICC-related clots by more than half, with no major bleeding
articles.title: Amrecibart and cenvacibart for the prevention of catheter-related thrombosis (ROXI-CATH): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
articles.population: 195 adults getting a PICC expected to stay at least 14 days, 12 centers in 6 countries
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to a single IV dose of amrecibart 300 mg, cenvacibart 250 mg or placebo, with ultrasounds at days 7 and 14. Venous thromboembolism by day 14 occurred in 20% with each antibody vs 43% with placebo (OR about 0.37 for both). There was no major bleeding in any group, and clinically relevant non-major bleeding was 3% in all three arms. Most clots were found by protocol ultrasound, the trial was industry funded (Regeneron), and it wasn't powered for clinical outcomes.
articles.why: Factor XI inhibition is moving closer to the clinic, and a single-dose agent would raise new questions about duration of effect and reversal. Good to have on the radar for patients with a PICC who present with bleeding or an arm clot in coming years.

articles.takeaway: More accepted pharmacist interventions were associated with better survival in a pediatric ICU
articles.title: Association of Cumulative Pharmacist Interventions and Interprofessional Adherence With Survival Among Patients Requiring Pharmacotherapeutic Optimization in a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Time-Dependent Cohort Study.
articles.population: 565 children with a PICU stay over 24 hours and at least one pharmacist intervention, 1 tertiary center, 2019–2021
articles.summary: Overall mortality was 11.9%, and the team accepted 72.2% of recommendations. Each additional cumulative intervention was tied to a small drop in the hazard of PICU death (HR 0.989, p = 0.040), and accepted interventions showed a somewhat stronger link (HR 0.983, p = 0.025), including in both surgical and non-surgical patients. Baseline illness severity remained the strongest predictor of death. Only patients who received an intervention were included, so there is no comparison to care without a pharmacist.
articles.why: Useful framing for justifying critical care and ED pharmacist positions: acceptance of recommendations, and not just their number, is what tracked with survival. The design can't prove causation.

articles.takeaway: A short dexamethasone course reduced nausea when starting oral morphine in opioid-naive cancer patients
articles.title: Prophylactic dexamethasone for prevention of opioid-induced nausea and vomiting in cancer patients: a randomised controlled trial (DEX-OINV Trial).
articles.population: 150 opioid-naive adults starting oral morphine, 1 tertiary cancer center
articles.summary: Patients got prophylactic oral dexamethasone (74) or no prophylaxis (76), with rescue antiemetics available in both arms. Mean nausea scores were lower with dexamethasone on day 1 (1.36 vs 2.93) and day 5 (0.74 vs 1.53), with a number needed to treat of 5 on day 1 for clinically meaningful nausea (adjusted OR 0.38). Vomiting fell on day 1 and no serious adverse events occurred. The open-label design and subjective outcome leave room for bias.
articles.why: A cheap option worth knowing for oncology patients started on opioids at ED discharge, but steroid effects on glucose and infection risk should be weighed. The result doesn't extend to non-cancer patients.

issues.note: A stronger window than most: one Lancet RCT in cardiogenic shock, three new intra-arterial tenecteplase trials and a small septic shock fluid RCT. The other picks are observational or meta-analytic, and the medetomidine item is a preprint that hasn't been peer reviewed.
bottom_line: Adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase took a hit: it didn't improve 90-day outcomes during thrombectomy (BRETIS-TNK2), and a basilar trial (INSIST-IT) stopped early for safety and lack of efficacy, with numerically more deaths.

In MI with cardiogenic shock, cangrelor reliably inhibited platelets where crushed ticagrelor mostly didn't, but it didn't prove non-inferior on 30-day clinical outcomes. Better platelet numbers haven't yet become better outcomes.

Medetomidine appeared in about 25% of Southern California fentanyl samples by August 2026, up from about 6% in May 2025. Naloxone won't reverse its sedation or bradycardia, so plan for it in overdoses that stay sedated.

articles.takeaway: In MI with cardiogenic shock, cangrelor beat crushed ticagrelor on platelet inhibition but missed non-inferiority on clinical outcomes
articles.title: Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial.
articles.population: 605 adults with MI complicated by cardiogenic shock, 29 hospitals in 5 European countries
articles.summary: Patients got cangrelor (30 mcg/kg bolus, then 4 mcg/kg/min for at least 2 hours) or crushed ticagrelor 180 mg. In the roughly 20% of patients with platelet testing, a platelet reactivity index under 50% at the end of PCI was reached in 100% with cangrelor vs 22% with ticagrelor. Death, MI or ischemic stroke at 30 days occurred in 38% vs 41%, but non-inferiority wasn't shown against a very tight 1-point margin (difference −4 points, 90% CI −10 to 3). Major bleeding was 6% vs 5%.
articles.why: Gut absorption is unreliable in shock, so an IV P2Y12 inhibitor makes pharmacologic sense, but this trial doesn't prove it improves outcomes. If cangrelor is used, plan the oral transition: ticagrelor can be loaded during or right after the infusion, while clopidogrel or prasugrel must wait until it stops.

articles.takeaway: Limiting fluid boluses by bedside intolerance signals improved oxygenation in septic shock, but the trial stopped early at 35 patients
articles.title: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial.
articles.population: 35 ventilated adults with fluid-responsive septic shock and high risk of fluid harm, 3 Chilean ICUs
articles.summary: Before each bolus, lung ultrasound, VExUS, E/e' and CVP were graded as green (500 mL), yellow (250 mL) or red (no fluid), compared with standard 500-mL boluses over a 6-hour window. The intervention arm got less protocol fluid (250 vs 650 mL), and PaO2:FiO2 rose by a median of 40.5 points vs a fall of 37.9 (between-group difference +78). Lactate and capillary refill changes didn't differ. Only 36 of 62 planned patients were enrolled, cumulative fluid was similar between groups, and the authors call the effect uncertain.
articles.why: A concept to watch rather than a protocol to adopt: fluid responsive doesn't mean fluid tolerant. It supports reassessing before every bolus in boarded septic shock patients and starting norepinephrine early rather than defaulting to more volume.

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy didn't improve 90-day function in large-vessel stroke
articles.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke: the BRETIS-TNK2 trial.
articles.population: 380 patients with large-vessel occlusion eligible for thrombectomy within 24 hours, multicenter open-label trial
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy or thrombectomy alone. A modified Rankin Scale score of 0–2 at 90 days occurred in 40.0% with tenecteplase vs 46.8% with thrombectomy alone (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.50–1.14; P = 0.19). The numbers leaned against tenecteplase, though the difference wasn't significant.
articles.why: Tempers recent enthusiasm for routine IA lytics. Earlier digests covered benefit after thrombectomy in selected patients, while this trial tested giving it during the procedure. A separate phase 2 trial this window (RESCUE-TNK, PMID 42995180) improved reperfusion in medium-vessel occlusion (61% vs 28%), so patient selection may be the deciding factor.

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase after basilar thrombectomy didn't help and the trial stopped early for safety and futility
articles.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase for acute basilar artery occlusion with sufficient recanalization after thrombectomy: the INSIST-IT randomized clinical trial.
articles.population: 144 patients with basilar occlusion and successful reperfusion within 24 hours of onset, multicenter open-label trial
articles.summary: Independent ambulation (mRS 0–3) at 90 days occurred in 40.0% with adjunctive tenecteplase vs 50.0% with standard therapy (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.34–1.29). Symptomatic ICH was similar (6.2% vs 4.8%), but 90-day mortality was numerically higher (41.3% vs 26.5%; OR 1.96, 95% CI 0.97–4.03; P = 0.063). The safety monitoring committee recommended stopping for safety concerns and lack of efficacy.
articles.why: A caution against extending anterior-circulation IA lytic data to basilar occlusions. Pharmacists asked to prepare post-thrombectomy IA tenecteplase should confirm the indication and location rather than assume a class benefit.

articles.takeaway: TXA in severe pelvic fractures was linked to lower 24-hour mortality, but not to less massive transfusion
articles.title: Association of tranexamic acid with early death or massive transfusion after severe pelvic ring fractures: A nationwide registry-based cohort study.
articles.population: 5,288 adults with blunt severe pelvic ring fractures, Japan Trauma Data Bank, 2019–2023
articles.summary: With overlap weighting, death within 24 hours or massive transfusion occurred in 13.0% with TXA vs 18.1% without (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60–0.87). The result came from 24-hour mortality (RR 0.62), since massive transfusion alone didn't differ (RR 0.94) and any transfusion was more common with TXA. Timing of TXA wasn't available, and the association weakened when outcome time origins were aligned (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65–1.00).
articles.why: Doesn't change the CRASH-2 approach for bleeding trauma: TXA 1 g over 10 minutes within 3 hours, then 1 g over 8 hours. It does not establish a pelvic-specific benefit, so timing and early hemorrhage control still matter most.

articles.takeaway: Balanced fluids resolved DKA about 4 hours faster than saline, but lactated Ringer's carried hyperkalemia and AKI signals
articles.title: Effectiveness of various balanced electrolyte solutions in the resuscitation of patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: A pairwise meta-analysis and network meta-analysis.
articles.population: 18 studies comparing balanced solutions with saline; 16 studies in the network analysis
articles.summary: Compared with normal saline, balanced solutions shortened time to DKA resolution (mean difference −4.41 hours) and hospital stay (−0.43 days), with higher bicarbonate and lower chloride after resuscitation, though heterogeneity was significant. Lactated Ringer's (−2.60 hours) and Sterofundin (−4.30 hours) both shortened resolution vs saline. Hyperkalemia (OR 4.06) and AKI (OR 2.26) were more common with LR than saline, and comparisons between balanced fluids were indirect.
articles.why: Adds support for a balanced crystalloid in adult DKA. The LR safety signal comes from indirect, low-precision data, so keep following potassium closely while insulin runs. Sterofundin isn't marketed in the US, so Plasma-Lyte or LR are the practical options here.

articles.takeaway: Medetomidine rose to about a quarter of Southern California fentanyl samples within about 15 months
articles.title: Characterizing the Emergence of Medetomidine in Southern California Fentanyl Markets.
articles.population: Community drug-checking samples, Southern California, 2023–2026 (22 quantified; 13 tested for enantiomers)
articles.summary: Mass spectrometry of voluntarily submitted samples showed medetomidine co-present with fentanyl in about 6% of samples in May 2025, the month it was first detected, rising to about 25% by August 2026. Mean concentration was 0.4% by mass, often with lidocaine and xylazine. All 13 samples tested were racemic, which suggests the drug wasn't diverted from pharmaceutical dexmedetomidine. This preprint has not been peer reviewed, and drug-checking samples aren't a random sample of the supply.
articles.why: Medetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist, so expect sedation and bradycardia that outlast naloxone's effect, and possibly a severe withdrawal syndrome. Routine urine screens won't detect it, and medetomidine is now spreading beyond the eastern US.

articles.takeaway: Best available antibiotics within 24 hours cut 14-day mortality in MDR gram-negative bacteremia, mainly for 3GC-resistant organisms
articles.title: Early best available antibiotic therapy for multidrug-resistant gram-negative bloodstream infections: a target trial emulation.
articles.population: 1,412 adults with MDR gram-negative bloodstream infection, 19 Asian countries (ACORN-HAI), 2022–2025
articles.summary: Guideline-recommended therapy started within 24 hours of blood culture was associated with lower 14-day mortality (18.5% vs 25.6%; risk difference −7.1%, 95% CI −11.3 to −3.0). The benefit was clear for third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (−7.4%), and larger in severe infections. Estimates for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales and Acinetobacter were uncertain, and most of that therapy was polymyxin-based.
articles.why: Supports reviewing prior cultures and risk factors at the first ED dose, and using a carbapenem early when ESBL risk is high. Speed alone may not rescue carbapenem-resistant infections treated with polymyxins, where agent choice also matters.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window. The EM picks are a pharmacist-led stewardship study, two meta-analyses, a prospective analgesia cohort, a trauma tox study and a reversal-agent review, with two stewardship papers rounding it out. Read the observational items as practice context.
bottom_line: Intranasal opioids (fentanyl or similar) relieved acute pain as well as IV morphine at 20 and 30 minutes, with no extra adverse events, so you don't need to wait on an IV line to treat pain.
When ED pharmacists owned MRSA nasal PCR ordering for admitted pneumonia patients, anti-MRSA therapy dropped from about 6 hours to about 1 hour with no change in readmissions or mortality.
In trauma patients, most positive fentanyl screens reflected fentanyl the team had already given. Check the MAR before calling a urine drug screen evidence of pre-injury use.

articles.takeaway: Pharmacist-ordered MRSA nasal PCR in the ED cut anti-MRSA therapy for pneumonia from ~6 h to ~1 h
articles.title: Impact of MRSA nasal PCR in the emergency department on duration of vancomycin and linezolid for pneumonia.
articles.population: 200 adults with suspected pneumonia given anti-MRSA therapy in the ED and admitted, 1 US academic center
articles.summary: ED pharmacists took responsibility for ordering the MRSA nasal swab under an existing hospital protocol, and ED nurses collected it before the patient left the department. Median duration of vancomycin or linezolid fell from 5.9 hours before the change to 1.1 hours after it (p = 0.006). PCR ordering rose from 69% to 86%, which was not statistically significant, and length of stay, 30-day readmission and 30-day mortality didn't differ. It is a single-center pre-post design without a randomized control.
articles.why: A cheap, high-yield ED pharmacist task: order the nasal PCR with the first vancomycin dose so a negative result (NPV over 95% for MRSA pneumonia) can stop it before the patient reaches the floor.

articles.takeaway: Intranasal opioids matched IV morphine for acute moderate-to-severe pain at 20 and 30 minutes
articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Intranasal Opioids vs. Intravenous Morphine for Acute Moderate-to-Severe Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.population: 10 RCTs, 1,164 adults and children with acute pain in ED, prehospital, procedural or postoperative settings
articles.summary: Pain score reductions at 20 minutes (SMD −0.05) and 30 minutes (SMD −0.05) were essentially identical between intranasal opioids and IV morphine, with little heterogeneity. Rescue analgesia was also equal (RR 1.00). Overall adverse events, serious adverse events, respiratory events, hypotension, GI effects, dizziness and rhinorrhea didn't differ, and only altered taste was borderline more common with the intranasal route. The trials were small, so rare serious events can't be excluded.
articles.why: Supports intranasal fentanyl (often 1.5–2 mcg/kg, max about 100 mcg per dose, using a concentrated solution and an atomizer) as a first-line option for kids, fractures and patients without IV access. Split volumes above about 1 mL between nostrils.

articles.takeaway: Brivaracetam stopped status epilepticus in about half of patients as a second-line drug
articles.title: Brivaracetam for the termination of status epilepticus: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 10 observational studies of patients with status epilepticus given brivaracetam
articles.summary: The pooled response rate was 52% (95% CI 45–59%), with moderate heterogeneity. Studies differed in how many antiseizure drugs had failed first, how long seizures had lasted before brivaracetam, and the loading and maintenance doses used. Response looked better when brivaracetam was given within 24 hours at loading doses of about 200–300 mg. No comparative RCTs were available, so it can't yet be ranked against levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.
articles.why: Brivaracetam can be pushed IV quickly and has fewer behavioral effects than levetiracetam, but it costs more and lacks trial data. For now it is an alternative second-line agent, not a replacement for levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4,500 mg).

articles.takeaway: Idarucizumab remains the only dabigatran antidote, but its benefit rests on single-arm and observational data
articles.title: A safety profile on idarucizumab for dabigatran reversal: an update.
articles.population: Review of pharmacology, clinical and real-world evidence for idarucizumab
articles.summary: The authors summarize idarucizumab's pharmacology, the evidence behind it and practical points on giving it and caring for patients afterward. Its clinical benefit is supported only by the single-arm RE-VERSE AD trial and observational studies, with no comparator. They note that high cost and falling dabigatran use make routine stocking hard to justify in rural or resource-limited sites, that trial bleeding definitions don't map neatly onto real cases, and that follow-up care and anticoagulation stewardship after reversal deserve more attention.
articles.why: For dabigatran bleeds, give idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials). If it isn't stocked, 4F-PCC or hemodialysis are fallbacks. Plan when and how to restart anticoagulation once bleeding is controlled.

articles.takeaway: About 63% of positive fentanyl screens in trauma patients were linked to fentanyl the team had given
articles.title: Administered opioids and benzodiazepines and the interpretation of positive trauma urine drug screens.
articles.population: 1,420 trauma patients with a urine drug screen, 1 US Level II trauma center, 2023–2024
articles.summary: Fentanyl screens were positive in 70% of patients given fentanyl before urine collection vs 12.5% of those who weren't (aOR 15.3), and the result held when only prehospital doses were counted. Similar but smaller effects were seen for opiates (aOR 5.9) and benzodiazepines (aOR 6.1), while cocaine, cannabis and amphetamine screens weren't affected. Modeling estimated that 63% of fentanyl, 34% of opiate and 29% of benzodiazepine positives were associated with drugs given during care.
articles.why: Reconcile every positive screen against the EMS run sheet and MAR before it lands in the chart as substance use. Know which agents each immunoassay channel picks up (e.g., hydromorphone and oxycodone vary by assay).

articles.takeaway: Persistent pain at 2 weeks, not opioid use, predicted new chronic pain after ED discharge
articles.title: Early Post-Discharge Pain Persistence, Not Opioid Use, Is Associated with New-Onset Chronic Pain Among Opioid-Naive Emergency Department Patients: A Secondary Analysis of a Prospective Cohort.
articles.population: 483 opioid-naive adults discharged from 2 urban US EDs with a new opioid prescription for pain
articles.summary: At 6 months, 26.7% had developed new chronic pain (pain on more than half of days). Neck or back pain and longer pain before the ED visit predicted it. Pain that persisted at 2 weeks (OR 2.36) and moderate or severe pain at 2 weeks (OR 2.20) were associated with new chronic pain, while opioid use at 48 hours or 2 weeks was not. About 20% of the original cohort was lost to follow-up.
articles.why: The 2-week mark is a useful checkpoint: patients still in pain then need follow-up and a multimodal plan (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, PT), not more opioid refills. Keep ED opioid prescriptions short.

articles.takeaway: Extended-infusion pip-tazo may improve clinical cure in critically ill adults, but mortality benefit is unproven
articles.title: Prolonged Versus Intermittent Piperacillin-Tazobactam Infusion in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
articles.population: 7 RCTs, 6,080 critically ill adults (BLING III supplied most of the patients)
articles.summary: Prolonged (extended or continuous) infusion improved clinical cure (RR 1.23) across 6 small trials, but certainty was very low. The 90-day mortality estimate leaned toward benefit without reaching significance (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84–1.01), and BLING III carried 99% of the weight. Effects on 28-day mortality and antibiotic duration were uncertain. The authors conclude that the results fit the class-wide beta-lactam data but don't prove a pip-tazo-specific mortality benefit.
articles.why: Give the first pip-tazo dose in the ED as a 30-minute bolus so it isn't delayed, then switch to extended infusion (e.g., 4.5 g over 4 hours every 8 hours). Watch for Y-site incompatibilities when lines are crowded.

articles.takeaway: Turning off cross-reactivity alerts plus an allergy guideline raised beta-lactam use with no added reactions
articles.title: Impact of multimodal interventions on β-lactam use in patients with penicillin or cephalosporin allergy.
articles.population: 234 hospitalized adults with a documented penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, 1 US center
articles.summary: The intervention combined suppressing EHR beta-lactam cross-reactivity alerts, clinician education and a new beta-lactam allergy guideline. Penicillin or cephalosporin use rose from 65% to 81% (p = 0.006), and non-beta-lactam use fell from 27% to 14%. Allergic reactions, C. difficile infection, length of stay and stopping antibiotics for intolerance didn't differ. It is a small single-center pre-post study.
articles.why: Most penicillin-allergic ED patients can safely get cefazolin or a cephalosporin with a dissimilar side chain (e.g., ceftriaxone). Pharmacists can push the guideline and alert changes that make this the default.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window, so the EM picks are a large propensity-matched cohort, a systematic review and registry data. Two pharmacist-relevant AJHP studies and a JAMA newborn vitamin K cohort round it out.
bottom_line: For cannabinoid hyperemesis, reach for haloperidol or droperidol before ondansetron: either butyrophenone roughly halved 72-hour ED returns in a large matched cohort.

Rapid methadone titration (e.g., 30–40 mg start, +10 mg every 3–4 h to 50–80 mg on day 1) had no reported deaths in fentanyl-era or inpatient studies, which supports faster starts for ED-initiated or boarded OUD patients.
In children admitted with CAP, waiting past 4 hours for antibiotics didn't worsen outcomes, so stable kids can be observed rather than reflexively treated in the ED.

articles.takeaway: Haloperidol or droperidol cut 72-hour ED returns for cannabinoid hyperemesis by about half vs ondansetron
