articles.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Haloperidol, Droperidol, and Ondansetron for Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome in the Emergency Department.
articles.population: Adult ED visits with a suspected CHS phenotype, TriNetX multicenter network, 2014–2024
articles.summary: Researchers made three propensity-matched pairwise comparisons of drugs given at the index ED visit. Return to the ED within 72 hours was lower with haloperidol than ondansetron (8.2% vs 15.1%; OR 0.50) and with droperidol than ondansetron (7.4% vs 14.0%; OR 0.49), while haloperidol and droperidol didn't differ (OR 0.75, not significant). In adjusted survival models, both butyrophenones independently predicted fewer returns and ondansetron did not, and coded adverse events were rare. It is retrospective, diagnosis-code based and lacks dose data.
articles.why: Supports putting haloperidol (often 2.5–5 mg IV/IM) or droperidol ahead of ondansetron on CHS order sets. Check a QTc and screen for other QT-prolonging drugs, and pair with counseling on cannabis cessation and topical capsaicin.

articles.takeaway: Rapid methadone titration protocols looked safe, with no deaths in fentanyl-era or inpatient studies
articles.title: Safety and effectiveness of rapid methadone titration protocols in opioid use disorder: A systematic review.
articles.population: 29 studies, 16,154 patients with OUD starting methadone, inpatient and outpatient settings
articles.summary: The most common protocol started at 30–40 mg and added 10 mg every 3–4 hours as needed, up to 50–80 mg on day 1, with day-7 doses of roughly 53–97 mg in the larger studies. Across the 18 fentanyl-era studies and the 18 inpatient studies that reported mortality, no deaths occurred; nearly all reported deaths came from two older case series built from coroner reports. Overdose was under 1% and sedation was usually mild. Heterogeneity prevented pooling, and overall evidence quality was low.
articles.why: Fentanyl tolerance makes slow 'start low, go slow' methadone starts leave patients in withdrawal for weeks. Pharmacists can help design monitored rapid-titration protocols for admitted or boarded OUD patients, with sedation checks before each extra dose and QTc review.

articles.takeaway: Major bleeding hit 3% of acute PE patients in 30 days and 13% after thrombolysis
articles.title: Major bleeding in patients with acute pulmonary embolism: results from the COPE study.
articles.population: 5,213 patients with acute PE, prospective multicenter Italian COPE study
articles.summary: ISTH major bleeding occurred in 3.1% within 30 days, split about evenly between early (under 7 days) and late events. Bleeding occurred in 12.9% of patients given thrombolysis vs 2.5% of those who weren't. Active cancer, prior bleeding, dementia, anemia, syncope and thrombolysis predicted early bleeding, while cancer, prior bleeding and anemia predicted late bleeding. Four clinical bleeding phenotypes predicted risk about as well as PE-SARD, BACS and VTE-Bleed.
articles.why: Puts a number on the lytic bleeding trade-off for ED PE decisions. Flag cancer, anemia and prior bleeding when choosing between systemic lytics, reduced-dose regimens or catheter-directed therapy, and keep reversal agents ready.

articles.takeaway: For children admitted with pneumonia, antibiotics within 4 hours didn't reduce escalation of care
articles.title: Time to antibiotics and outcomes for children hospitalized with community acquired pneumonia.
articles.population: 758 children (3 months to 18 years) admitted from the ED with suspected CAP, 4 US children's hospitals
articles.summary: About 59% got antibiotics within 4 hours of ED arrival. In inverse propensity-weighted models, escalation of care (more respiratory support, ICU transfer, vasopressors or a chest tube) didn't differ between early and later antibiotics (3% vs 2%; OR 1.46, wide CI). Length of stay, oxygen duration and cost also didn't differ. Events were few, so a small effect can't be excluded, and septic children aren't the target of this finding.
articles.why: Supports a period of observation for well-appearing children with possible viral pneumonia instead of reflexive ED antibiotics. When treatment is needed, amoxicillin or ampicillin remains the narrow-spectrum default.

articles.takeaway: Milrinone in pediatric fluid-refractory septic shock was linked to higher mortality and more cardiac arrests
articles.title: Fluid-Refractory Septic Shock in Children and Milrinone: Outcomes in a Two-Center, Retrospective Cohort in France, 2011-2021.
articles.population: 290 children with fluid-refractory septic shock on vasoactive drugs, 2 French PICUs
articles.summary: Milrinone was used in 16% of children, at a median of 0.5 mcg/kg/min. It was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR 2.57), more fluid boluses, more mechanical ventilation, more PICU cardiac arrests (48% vs 11%) and more adverse events. Milrinone was likely given to sicker children with cardiac dysfunction, so confounding by indication is a major limitation.
articles.why: Milrinone's vasodilation and long, renally cleared half-life can worsen hypotension in warm or vasoplegic shock. Reserve it for documented low cardiac output with adequate pressure, and favor epinephrine as the first inotrope.

articles.takeaway: AUC-guided vancomycin monitoring cut AKI risk by about a third vs trough-guided monitoring
articles.title: Still Chasing the Curve: Updated Evidence on Vancomycin AUC vs Trough Monitoring and Its Impact on AKI. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, 2020-2025.
articles.population: 80 studies, 27,067 patients; 30 direct comparisons (18,146 patients) published 2020–2025
articles.summary: In head-to-head studies, AUC-guided monitoring lowered AKI risk compared with trough-guided monitoring (RR 0.66), and the result held when restricted to KDIGO-defined AKI. Mortality (OR 0.83) and 30-day readmission (OR 0.95) didn't differ, though few studies reported them. Heterogeneity was moderate (I² 64%), and most included studies were observational.
articles.why: Reinforces the 2020 consensus guideline: start vancomycin from the ED with a weight-based load, then hand off to an AUC (400–600) Bayesian or two-level protocol rather than trough targets.

articles.takeaway: Starting an NSAID while on a GLP-1 RA didn't raise GI bleed or ulcer risk vs SGLT2i or DPP-4i
articles.title: NSAID initiation and risk for gastrointestinal bleeding in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.population: 68,881 veterans with type 2 diabetes starting an NSAID on a GLP-1 RA (13,433), SGLT2i or DPP-4i
articles.summary: One-year GI bleed or ulcer rates were about 1% in all three groups (0.9% with GLP-1 RAs). After adjustment, GLP-1 RA users had no higher risk than SGLT2i users (HR 0.85) or DPP-4i users (HR 0.82), and results were similar for GI bleeding alone. The population was mostly older men, and over-the-counter NSAID use wasn't captured.
articles.why: A common ED discharge question. A GLP-1 RA alone shouldn't stop a short NSAID course, but the usual GI risk factors (age, anticoagulants, prior ulcer, steroids) still call for a PPI or an alternative analgesic.

articles.takeaway: Newborn vitamin K refusal more than doubled to 6.8%, and refusers had over twice the intracranial bleeding risk
articles.title: Nonreceipt of Newborn Vitamin K and Risk of Bleeding.
articles.population: 5,240,780 infants born at 35–43 weeks, US hospitals in all 50 states, 2017–2025
articles.summary: Nonreceipt of intramuscular vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who didn't get it had more bleeding by 6 months (288 vs 186 per 10,000; adjusted RR 1.47), more intracranial bleeding (33 vs 13 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.43) and more deaths with bleeding during the birth stay (adjusted RR 2.69). Bleeding was identified from diagnosis codes, which may misclassify some events.
articles.why: Infants with late vitamin K deficiency bleeding present to the ED with lethargy, vomiting or seizures. Ask about vitamin K at birth, and know the treatment: IV or subcutaneous vitamin K 1 mg plus 4-factor PCC or FFP for life-threatening bleeds.

issues.note: A thin window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue leans on large observational ED datasets plus one systematic review and one NEJM trial. Read the cohorts as practice context rather than practice-changers.
bottom_line: Bystander naloxone works: when a layperson gave it before EMS arrived, EMS needed to give more naloxone less often and transported fewer patients. Keep handing out kits at ED discharge.
Nearly half of intoxicated ED patients had at least one electrolyte abnormality. If potassium is low, check magnesium and phosphate too, and replete magnesium before chasing potassium.
About 1 in 7 adults admitted from the ED with influenza still left without an antiviral. Start oseltamivir in the ED for every admitted flu patient, regardless of symptom duration.

articles.takeaway: Layperson naloxone before EMS arrival meant less repeat naloxone and fewer transports than first-responder naloxone
articles.title: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose.
articles.population: 26,087 EMS activations for opioid overdose with naloxone given before EMS arrival, US national 2023 dataset
articles.summary: About 31% of patients got naloxone from a layperson and the rest from trained responders such as police or firefighters. After a layperson dose, EMS gave more naloxone less often (24.4% vs 34.8%; aOR 0.73) and transported fewer patients (79.4% vs 84.4%; aOR 0.78). Advanced airways (about 1.5%) and cardiac arrest (about 6%) were uncommon and similar between groups. The data are cross-sectional, so patient severity and refusals can't be fully separated.
articles.why: Supports ED naloxone kit distribution and take-home programs. Also a reminder that more patients may decline transport after bystander reversal, so long-acting opioid exposures can be missed.

articles.takeaway: In severe hyperkalemia (K 7.0 or higher), kidney function, not the potassium value, predicted urgent dialysis
articles.title: Severe Hyperkalemia in the Emergency Department: Factors Associated with Dialysis and Mortality.
articles.population: 378 non-dialysis adults with plasma K of 7.0 mmol/L or higher in the ED, 1 center, 2010–2024
articles.summary: About half of patients had an ECG abnormality and 28% had severe ECG changes, and higher potassium was tied to more ECG changes. Urgent dialysis was needed in 12.2% and was predicted by stage III AKI, stage V CKD and younger age, not by the admission potassium after adjustment. In-hospital mortality was 23% and tracked with older age, malignancy, female sex and MAP below 70 mmHg.
articles.why: Calcium, insulin with dextrose, and beta-agonists still come first, but this supports calling nephrology early for patients with advanced CKD or severe AKI rather than waiting on repeat potassium levels.

articles.takeaway: About half of ED ethanol intoxication visits had an electrolyte abnormality; low K flagged low Mg and phosphate
articles.title: Incidence of Electrolyte Abnormalities in Emergency Department Patients Presenting With Ethanol Intoxication.
articles.population: 223,456 VA ED visits (83,178 patients) with serum ethanol above 50 mg/dL, 2010–2019
articles.summary: At least one electrolyte abnormality was found in 48.8% of encounters, and 2.9% had a severe one. Hypokalemia roughly doubled to tripled the odds of hypomagnesemia (OR 2.64) and hypophosphatemia (OR 2.51). The population was 94% male veterans, which limits generalizability.
articles.why: Argues against skipping labs in clinically intoxicated patients. Pair a basic panel with Mg and phosphate when K is low, and add thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients.

articles.takeaway: About 86% of adults admitted with influenza got an antiviral in the ED, with gaps by region and demographics
articles.title: Changes in Antiviral Treatment for Hospitalized Adults with Influenza in United States Emergency Departments.
articles.population: 483,459 adults hospitalized from US EDs with influenza, 2016–2025
articles.summary: Overall, 86.3% received oseltamivir, peramivir, baloxavir or zanamivir in the ED, with a low of 72.7% in 2021 and 85.1% in 2025. Treatment was less likely in the West (OR 0.78) and South (OR 0.95) than in the Northeast, and differed by age, race, ethnicity and language. ED treatment rates rose and fell with national flu positivity (r = 0.59).
articles.why: Guidelines recommend antivirals for every hospitalized flu patient, even after 48 hours of symptoms. An ED pharmacist prompt or order-set default is an easy fix for the remaining gap.

articles.takeaway: Low-level pyuria drove a large share of unnecessary antibiotics for suspected pediatric UTI
articles.title: Low-Level Pyuria and Antibiotic Prescribing for Suspected Urinary Tract Infection in Children.
articles.population: 1,150 children (2 months to 17 years) with urinalysis at ED and urgent care visits, 4 Northern California sites, 2022–2023
articles.summary: Overall, 16.6% of children got empiric antibiotics. Low-level pyuria (trace leukocyte esterase or a few WBCs) raised the odds of starting antibiotics more than sixfold (aOR 6.62) compared with no pyuria. It accounted for about 17% of overtreatment in children whose cultures ruled out UTI, but only about 2% of appropriate treatment for confirmed UTI.
articles.why: Trace pyuria alone shouldn't trigger antibiotics. ED culture-callback programs run by pharmacists can stop unneeded courses once cultures come back negative.

articles.takeaway: Probenecid-boosted once-daily cefazolin performed like ceftriaxone for cellulitis needing IV therapy
articles.title: Addition of probenecid to beta-lactam antibiotics in the treatment of skin and soft tissue infections: a systematic review.
articles.population: 9 studies, more than 1,600 patients with SSTI
articles.summary: Most studies compared once-daily IV cefazolin plus oral probenecid with ceftriaxone or more frequent cefazolin. Treatment success, failure, relapse and admission rates were similar. Evidence for oral beta-lactams plus probenecid was thin but didn't suggest they were worse. Adverse events were reported inconsistently and were mostly GI, possibly more common with probenecid.
articles.why: A narrower-spectrum option for ED-to-outpatient IV cellulitis pathways (e.g., cefazolin 2 g plus probenecid 1 g daily). Check for renal impairment and drug interactions, such as methotrexate, before adding probenecid.

articles.takeaway: Dexmedetomidine caused hypotension or more vasopressor need in most ICU patients with RV dysfunction
articles.title: Safety of Dexmedetomidine Use in Adult ICU Patients With Right Ventricular Dysfunction.
articles.population: 245 ICU adults with echo-confirmed RV dysfunction given dexmedetomidine, 1 US center, 2017–2022
articles.summary: A composite adverse event (bradycardia, hypotension, higher vasopressor or inotrope needs, or asystole) occurred in 62.4% of patients after dexmedetomidine was started. Hypotension was the most common event, and about 20% needed more vasopressor support (mean rise of 0.06 mcg/kg/min norepinephrine equivalents). Event rates were similar across mild, moderate and severe RV dysfunction, and there was no comparison group.
articles.why: Relevant to boarded ED patients with PE, pulmonary hypertension or RV failure after intubation. Start low, skip the loading dose, and have a vasopressor ready if you choose dexmedetomidine.

articles.takeaway: Plozasiran cut triglycerides by about 80% and acute pancreatitis by nearly 80% in severe hypertriglyceridemia
articles.title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis.
articles.population: 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia, SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 (multinational)
articles.summary: Patients were randomized 2:1 to subcutaneous plozasiran 25 mg or placebo every 3 months. At 12 months, median triglycerides fell 79–81% with plozasiran, about 45–47 percentage points more than placebo, and over 90% reached a level below 500 mg/dL vs about half on placebo. In pooled data, acute pancreatitis occurred at 1 vs 5 events per 100 patient-years (rate ratio 0.22). Adverse event rates were the same in both groups (73%).
articles.why: An APOC3-targeting siRNA given 4 times a year could prevent repeat hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis visits. Expect questions about it during ED med histories and discharge planning.

issues.note: Another light window with one ED drug RCT (topical TXA for epistaxis). The rest are meta-analyses, cohorts and a pharmacist-practice study, so read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Topical TXA applied directly to the bleeding site helped stop spontaneous nosebleeds that first aid didn't control. It's a cheap, low-dose ED adjunct, though it didn't clearly reduce 24-hour rebleeding.
ER guanfacine overdoses in teens cause near-universal bradycardia and hypotension. Supportive care with fluids, atropine as needed and cardiac monitoring was enough, and every patient recovered.
In ICU patients on carbapenems, doses above the renal-adjusted recommendation were tied to much more AKI. Re-check CrCl daily and adjust; don't leave the ED loading regimen running unchanged.

articles.takeaway: Topical TXA beat placebo for stopping refractory spontaneous nosebleeds in the ED, but didn't clearly cut rebleeding
articles.title: Effect of Topical Tranexamic Acid in Acute Spontaneous Epistaxis: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.population: 162 ED patients with spontaneous epistaxis not controlled by first aid (76 TXA, 86 placebo)
articles.summary: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, TXA was applied directly to the bleeding site. It achieved initial hemostasis in the ED more often than placebo (p = 0.047). Rebleeding within 24 hours was numerically lower but not significantly different (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.17–1.24), and significant rebleeding was rare in both groups (RR 1.50, wide CI). The trial was small and the result was borderline.
articles.why: Supports stocking a topical TXA option (often the IV 100 mg/mL solution on pledgets) for anterior epistaxis before packing. Pharmacists can standardize the concentration and how it's applied.

articles.takeaway: Pediatric ER guanfacine overdoses caused bradycardia and hypotension that responded to supportive care
articles.title: Extended-release guanfacine overdose in a pediatric emergency department: a systematic review and a 10-year retrospective chart review.
articles.population: 15 children at 1 tertiary pediatric ED over 10 years, plus 11 published pediatric cases
articles.summary: In the ED cohort (median age 14), 73% of ingestions were intentional, often in teens with psychiatric conditions. Nearly all patients had bradycardia and hypotension, and some had transient hypertension early on. Most got IV fluids (87%), 20% got atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, and 3 needed PICU care; none got naloxone and all recovered. In the published cases (mostly accidental ingestions in young children), naloxone had inconsistent effects.
articles.why: ER guanfacine is increasingly common in ADHD households. Expect delayed, prolonged alpha-2 effects from the extended-release form, and have atropine and fluids ready; naloxone is a low-yield adjunct at best.

articles.takeaway: Early tirofiban within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis improved 90-day outcomes in non-cardioembolic stroke
articles.title: Early antiplatelet therapy after intravenous thrombolysis in acute non-cardiogenic ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 4 studies, 1,394 patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke after IVT (2 RCTs: ASSET-IT, INSTANT)
articles.summary: In the two RCTs (1,191 patients), starting tirofiban within 24 hours of thrombolysis raised the odds of mRS 0–1 at 90 days compared with standard antiplatelet timing (OR 1.78). Symptomatic ICH (OR 1.19) and mortality (OR 0.84) didn't differ significantly, but the confidence interval for sICH was wide and events were few. Aspirin data came from only one small study.
articles.why: Current guidelines generally hold antiplatelets for 24 hours after lytics. If your stroke team starts using early tirofiban, pharmacists will need a dosing protocol and bleeding checks.

articles.takeaway: ED pharmacist medication review for complex chronic patients cut inappropriate prescribing by about 21%
articles.title: Transitional care from the emergency department: Impact of a comprehensive pharmacotherapy review in complex chronic patients.
articles.population: Complex chronic patients seen in the ED, 151 intervention and 151 control, 1 Spanish hospital
articles.summary: Pharmacists reconciled medications and did a full pharmacotherapy review within 24 hours of the ED visit (48 hours on weekends), sent reports to primary care at discharge, and followed up at 1 and 3 months. Compared with usual care, polypharmacy, anticholinergic burden, potentially inappropriate prescriptions and reconciliation errors all fell, with inappropriate prescribing down 20.6% (mostly drugs without an indication, benzodiazepines and antipsychotics). Physicians accepted 49% of recommendations, but healthcare use didn't change.
articles.why: Evidence for the ED pharmacist's role beyond resuscitation: med rec and deprescribing in frail, high-utilizer patients, with handoff to primary care.

articles.takeaway: Balanced fluids didn't beat normal saline for pediatric DKA resolution, length of stay or cerebral edema
articles.title: Fluid choice in pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 8 studies (RCTs and observational), 47,840 children with DKA
articles.summary: Among the RCTs, time to DKA resolution (MD 2.27 hours, not significant), hospital length of stay and PICU length of stay didn't differ between balanced electrolyte solutions and 0.9% saline. Cerebral edema and AKI risks also didn't differ, but those estimates came from very few events and had extremely wide confidence intervals. The authors conclude that the evidence can't show either fluid is better or safer.
articles.why: Either fluid is reasonable for pediatric DKA; follow your institution's protocol. This differs from the adult and pediatric sepsis data, where balanced fluids have a modest edge.

articles.takeaway: DOACs performed similarly to warfarin for recanalization and major bleeding in cerebral venous thrombosis
articles.title: Direct oral anticoagulants versus vitamin K antagonist-based standard care in cerebral venous thrombosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.population: 6 RCTs, 430 patients with cerebral venous thrombosis
articles.summary: Recanalization or radiological improvement at about 6 months didn't differ between DOACs and VKA-based care (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.81–1.09), and the result held after excluding a trial with weak randomization. Major bleeding was rare in both groups (2 of 188 with DOACs vs 4 of 190 with comparators; RR 0.60, wide CI). Trials were small and used different imaging outcomes.
articles.why: Supports transitioning CVT patients to a DOAC after initial heparin, which simplifies discharge. Avoid DOACs in antiphospholipid syndrome and pregnancy.

articles.takeaway: Continuous paralytics in ventilated sepsis patients didn't change mortality but lengthened ICU stay and raised VAP
articles.title: Impact of Neuromuscular Blocking Agents on Hospital Outcomes in Mechanically Ventilated Patients With Sepsis: Propensity Score Analyses of A Nationwide Sepsis Cohort.
articles.population: 1,255 ventilated adults with sepsis, 20 Korean hospitals (292 matched pairs)
articles.summary: About a quarter of patients got a continuous NMBA infusion within 3 days of ICU admission. In-hospital mortality didn't differ in either the weighted or the matched analysis (17.1% vs 18.8%). NMBA use was associated with ICU stays about 3 days longer and more ventilator-associated pneumonia (8.6% vs 4.5%), with trends toward longer ventilation. Residual confounding by severity is likely.
articles.why: Reinforces saving continuous paralysis for specific indications such as severe ARDS or ventilator dyssynchrony. For boarded ED patients after RSI, focus on adequate analgesia and sedation rather than routine paralytic drips.

articles.takeaway: Carbapenem doses above renal-adjusted recommendations were linked to much higher AKI risk in the ICU
articles.title: Carbapenem Renal Dose Discordance and Acute Kidney Injury in the Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.population: 490 ICU adults on carbapenems for 48 hours or more, 1 Vietnamese hospital
articles.summary: Sixteen percent of patients got at least 1 day of dosing above renal-adjusted recommendations based on Cockcroft-Gault CrCl. AKI occurred in 35.9% of those patients vs 4.4% with appropriate dosing (adjusted RR 8.1; 5.9 in matched pairs). The link with treatment failure didn't meet the corrected significance threshold. Reverse causation is possible, since AKI itself makes a fixed dose discordant.
articles.why: Makes the case for daily pharmacist renal dose review. Full doses for the first 24–48 hours of sepsis are still reasonable, but adjust once renal function is clearer.

issues.note: Another thin window: no ED drug RCTs were indexed, so this issue runs short (7 picks). The resuscitation items are a trial secondary analysis and a review, and the rest are observational, a trial protocol and pharmacovigilance data, so treat them as context rather than practice-changers.
bottom_line: At ED triage, older age, abnormal vitals, intentional ingestion and pesticides (especially paraquat) flagged the poisonings most likely to turn severe. Paraquat caused 60% of deaths.
Post-arrest temperature control: no subgroup of OHCA patients (by downtime or admission neuro exam) benefited from 33 °C over controlled normothermia, which supports fever prevention as the default.
In kids with severe drug anaphylaxis, antibiotics and NSAIDs dominate FAERS reports, and ceftriaxone was tied to the most deaths. Keep IM epinephrine ready when giving first doses in the ED.

articles.takeaway: Age, abnormal triage vitals, intentional ingestion and pesticides predicted severe poisoning; paraquat caused most deaths
articles.title: Prospective identification of risk factors for patients with severe acute poisoning in emergency departments in northern Taiwan.
articles.population: 2,470 ED patients with acute poisoning, 2 Taiwanese tertiary centers over 2 years
articles.summary: Prescription medications were the most common exposure category (32.5%), and ingestion was the main route. Severe poisoning (Poisoning Severity Score 3–4) occurred in 11.5%, and 3.1% died; paraquat accounted for about 60% of deaths, with warfarin, amphetamines, digoxin, benzodiazepines, CO and methotrexate among the other fatal agents. Older age, abnormal vital signs at triage, suicidal intent and pesticide ingestion independently predicted severe poisoning, and the findings held when vitals were removed from the model.
articles.why: Gives simple triage-level red flags for which overdoses need early tox consult and close monitoring. Several of the fatal agents (warfarin, digoxin, methotrexate) have specific antidotes the ED pharmacist should have ready: vitamin K/PCC, digoxin Fab and glucarpidase or leucovorin.

articles.takeaway: Pooled TTM and TTM2 data found no OHCA subgroup that benefited from 33 °C over normothermia
articles.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
articles.population: 2,789 adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, TTM and TTM2 trials (multinational)
articles.summary: The authors used machine-learning methods (causal forests and Bayesian trees) to look for patients who might benefit from hypothermia based on ischemia time, prehospital factors and the admission neuro exam. Six-month mortality was 49.4% with 33 °C vs 47.9% with controlled normothermia. Estimated individual treatment effects barely varied, and no subgroup showed a meaningful benefit for either 6-month mortality or poor functional outcome.
articles.why: Supports fever prevention rather than deep hypothermia as the default post-arrest strategy, which means less need for the heavy sedation, paralytics and shivering protocols that 33 °C requires.

articles.takeaway: ECPR patients clot and bleed at the same time, so anticoagulation needs individualized, frequently reassessed targets
articles.title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients.
articles.population: Adults receiving extracorporeal CPR for refractory cardiac arrest (evidence review)
articles.summary: An international ECLS expert group reviewed how ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation, platelet dysfunction and the circuit itself push ECPR patients toward both thrombosis and major bleeding. High-quality evidence is scarce, and most practice is borrowed from other ECMO populations, so center-to-center variation is large. The authors argue against fixed anticoagulation targets and favor individualized dosing guided by repeated clinical and lab assessment.
articles.why: As more EDs launch ECPR programs, the pharmacist often owns the heparin bolus at cannulation and the infusion that follows. This review is a good primer on why one aPTT or anti-Xa target won't fit every patient.

articles.takeaway: Mayo's BLOOM trial is testing EHR-guided, individualized cefepime dosing in the first hours of sepsis
articles.title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol.
articles.population: Target of 300 or more critically ill adults starting cefepime for sepsis, Mayo Clinic Rochester (cluster-randomized)
articles.summary: Standard cefepime dosing produces 10- to 30-fold variation in drug exposure in critical illness, and up to 70% of patients may have low levels early on. The BLOOM-1 trial uses a population PK model based on weight and eGFR from both creatinine and cystatin C, delivered through EHR decision support, and compares it with usual dosing. Patients with AKI, dialysis or ECMO are excluded, and the trial measures feasibility, fidelity and exploratory PK and clinical outcomes, with enrollment expected to finish in January 2027.
articles.why: Shows where empiric beta-lactam dosing is heading: model-informed doses that balance under-exposure against cefepime neurotoxicity. Ordering a cystatin C with the sepsis workup may become part of the ED pharmacist's dosing workflow.

articles.takeaway: Diagnostic uncertainty roughly doubled the odds of antibiotics for viral fevers in the pediatric ED
articles.title: Predictors of Antibiotic Overuse in Febrile Children: A Sub-analysis of the Prospective, Multicenter AutoPilot-Dx Study.
articles.population: 1,008 febrile children (90 days to 18 years) in pediatric EDs, multicenter Germany, Italy and Israel
articles.summary: Among 628 children whose illness was adjudicated as viral by panel testing, 186 (about 30%) still received antibiotics. Physician-reported diagnostic uncertainty (OR 2.09), nonexudative tonsillitis (OR 2.78) and rales (OR 1.82) independently predicted overuse. Having a diagnostic test result at presentation was not associated with less overuse.
articles.why: Stewardship in the ED is largely about reducing uncertainty at the moment of decision. Pharmacists can push for Centor or McIsaac scoring with strep testing before treating sore throats, and for watchful-waiting prescriptions.

articles.takeaway: Antibiotics and NSAIDs drove most pediatric severe anaphylaxis reports, and ceftriaxone was linked to the most deaths
articles.title: Drugs associated with severe anaphylaxis in children and adolescents: a real-word FAERS pharmacovigilance study.
articles.population: FAERS reports of severe anaphylaxis in patients under 18, 2004–2023
articles.summary: Disproportionality analysis using five signal-detection methods found 138 drugs with positive signals. Anti-infectives had the most reports overall (845), ibuprofen was the single most-reported drug (369 cases), and ceftriaxone was associated with the most deaths. Signals for IV immunoglobulin and sevoflurane were not reflected in their labeling, and outcomes were worse in younger children. As with all spontaneous-report data, these are signals, not incidence rates.
articles.why: Common ED drugs (ceftriaxone, ibuprofen) top the list. Observe first IV antibiotic doses in kids, have weight-based IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg) ready, and document the reaction clearly.

articles.takeaway: Statins plus interacting antibiotics (mainly macrolides) about doubled the odds of muscle toxicity
articles.title: Drug-drug interactions between statins and antibiotics: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
articles.population: 3 observational studies of statin users with or without interacting antibiotics
articles.summary: Pooling three observational studies, concurrent use of interacting antibiotics (largely CYP3A4-inhibiting macrolides) with statins was associated with a higher risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis (pooled OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.82–2.50). The estimate was stable in leave-one-out analysis, but with only three studies the analysis can't separate risk by statin or antibiotic.
articles.why: A common ED discharge pitfall: clarithromycin or erythromycin with simvastatin, lovastatin or atorvastatin. Choose azithromycin or doxycycline, or hold the statin for the course.
